subtype: Approach: avoiding the decision through more meetings [Pitfall]
passage: Deepika called a fourth meeting about the new dashboard on a Monday in the Gurgaon office, opening with, 'Let's hear everyone once more.' Sales wanted the export tool first; the engineers wanted the security fix; support wanted a simpler screen. Each time, Deepika nodded and said she'd think about it, because choosing felt like telling two groups no. Three weeks went by. The release date slid past. Shankar, a senior engineer, stopped bringing a laptop to the meetings. Sales sent a curt email to management, and support began making their own workarounds. At the fifth meeting someone asked quietly, 'So who decided?' Deepika looked at her notes and had no answer. Everyone left annoyed, and none of the three requests was done.

qa.q: What did the engineers want first?
qa.a: The engineers wanted the security fix.

qa.q: Why does Deepika keep saying she will think about it?
qa.a: Choosing felt like telling two groups no, so Deepika avoids it, most likely out of fear of upsetting people.

qa.q: What other approach could Deepika use?
qa.a: Deepika could set a decision date, choose by agreed criteria such as customer impact and risk, and then explain the choice to each group.

qa.q: How does Shankar likely see the meetings?
qa.a: Shankar probably finds them a waste of time, shown by dropping the laptop, since the security fix is still waiting.

grounding: Shows a lead adding more meetings to avoid upsetting anyone, so the deadline passes and every group is unhappy.

subtype: Approach: avoiding the decision through more meetings [Pitfall]
passage:
'Another input meeting?' Mahima said, reading the invite. 'Ayesha, this is the fifth.'
'I just want to make sure design and support are comfortable,' Ayesha said.
'They told you in week one. Design wants the new layout, support wants the old one, and both said they'd live with either.'
'But if I pick one, the other will be upset.'
'And now?'
Ayesha didn't answer.
'The launch was on the 15th,' Mahima said. 'It's the 29th. Design thinks you don't trust their work. Support thinks you're hiding something. My team has been blocked for two weeks. And the client called me this morning, not you.'
'What did the client say?'
'That they'd rather have either version than none.'
Ayesha sat down slowly and cancelled the invite.

qa.q: When was the launch meant to be?
Why did Ayesha keep calling meetings, and what was the fear behind them?
qa.a: Ayesha was afraid that choosing one version would upset the other team, so another meeting felt safer than deciding.

qa.q: What approach would have suited Ayesha better in week one?
qa.a: Since both teams said they could live with either, Ayesha could have chosen, explained the reasons and set a date to review it.

qa.q: How does the delay look to Mahima's team?
qa.a: Mahima's team has been blocked for two weeks, frustrated that nothing moves while meetings pile up.

grounding: It shows a lead calling meeting after meeting to avoid upsetting anyone until the deadline is missed and every group is unhappy.

subtype: Approach: avoiding the decision through more meetings [Pitfall]
passage:
I'm Kunal, and I once missed a deadline by six weeks because I couldn't bear to disappoint anyone. We had to choose between two payment providers. Finance liked one, engineering the other. So I asked for more input. Then a comparison sheet. Then a call with each vendor, twice. Every time someone looked unhappy, I scheduled another meeting.
Chaitanya from engineering finally said in a corridor, 'Kunal, we'd accept either. What we can't accept is nothing.' By then, the contract with our old provider had lapsed, and we paid a penalty to extend it for a month. Finance blamed engineering, engineering blamed me, and both were right about something.
I learnt that avoiding a decision is still a decision. It's just one where everyone loses a little.

qa.q: By how long did Kunal miss the deadline?
Why did Kunal feel the need to schedule another meeting each time?
qa.a: Kunal couldn't bear to disappoint anyone, so each unhappy face made Kunal anxious enough to delay again.

qa.q: What could Kunal have done after the first comparison sheet?
qa.a: Kunal could have set a decision date, agreed points both teams accepted and chosen, explaining the reasons to the side that lost.

qa.q: How did the delay look to Chaitanya?
qa.a: Chaitanya was frustrated, since engineering would have accepted either provider but not endless waiting.

grounding: It shows a lead seeking more input to avoid upsetting anyone until the deadline passes and every group ends up unhappy.
